tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.

- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.description:
Search file contents using regular expressions (powered by ripgrep).

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always skipped for safety, even when `include_ignored` is `true`.

path.description: File or directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Omit to search the current working directory. Use Read instead when you already know a concrete file path and need its contents.

tools.description:
Read a text file from the local filesystem.

If the user provides a concrete file path to a text file, call Read directly. Do not `Glob`, `ls`, or otherwise pre-check known text file paths; missing or invalid file paths return errors you can handle. Do not use Read for directories; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob when you need files matching a name pattern (Glob lists files only, never directories). Use `Grep` only when the task is to search for unknown content or locations.

When you need several files, prefer to read them in parallel: emit multiple `Read` calls in a single response instead of reading one file per turn.

- Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.
- Returns up to 1000 lines or 100 KB per call, whichever comes first; lines longer than 2000 chars are truncated mid-line.
- Page larger files with `line_offset` (1-based start line) and `n_lines`. Omit `n_lines` to read up to the 1000-line cap.
- Sensitive files (`.env` files, credential stores, SSH private keys, and similar secrets) are refused to protect secrets; do not attempt to read them. Templates and public keys are exempt: `.env.example` / `.env.sample` / `.env.template` and public SSH keys such as `id_rsa.pub` read normally.
- Only UTF-8 text files can be read. Non-UTF-8 encodings, binary files, and files containing NUL bytes are refused; use `ReadMediaFile` for images or video, and Bash or an MCP tool for other binary formats.
- Negative line_offset reads from the end of the file (for example, -100 reads the last 100 lines); the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.
- Output format: `<line-number>\t<content>` per line.
- A `<system>...</system>` status block is appended after the file content; it summarizes how much was read (line and byte counts, truncation, line-ending notes) and is not part of the file itself.
- Pure CRLF files are displayed with LF line endings; `Edit` matches this output and preserves CRLF when writing back.
- Mixed or lone carriage-return line endings are shown as `\r` and require exact `Edit.old_string` escapes.
- After a successful `Edit`/`Write`, do not re-read solely to prove the write landed. When the task depends on an exact file, API, or output shape, inspect the final external contract before finishing.

path.description: Path to a text file. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute. Directories are not supported; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob for pattern search.

line_offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Omit to start at line 1. Negative values read from the end of the file; the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.

n_lines.description: The number of lines to read; the tool also applies its internal cap. Omit to read up to the internal cap of 1000 lines.

cat > /workspace/notes/06-errors.md <<'REPORT_EOF'
# lnav 0.14.0 — Error Handling & Messages (Area 06)

Binary: `/workspace/executable` (`lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`). All probes run on Linux as root,
stdout/stderr redirected to files (not TTYs). Unless noted otherwise: **no ANSI escape
bytes are emitted** even with `TERM=xterm-256color` when output is not a TTY.

## 1. Global message anatomy (non-TTY / headless)

All diagnostics go to **stderr** (except where noted). General shape:

```
  error: <summary>
 reason: <detail>
 --> <source>:<line>
 | <source line, space-padded to min width 40 after " | ">
 = help: <help text>
```

Exact prefixes (verified with `od -c` / `sed -n l`):

- `  error: ` — **two** leading spaces.
- ` reason: ` — **one** leading space.
- ` --> ` — one leading space, then `-->`, path, `:`, line number.
- ` | ` — one leading space, pipe, space, then source text. Source text is right-padded
  with spaces to a minimum total line width of 43 chars (i.e. content padded to 40);
  longer text is not padded.
- ` = help: ` / ` = note: ` — one leading space. Continuation lines of help are indented
  with spaces to align under the text after `= `.
- `  info: ` — two leading spaces (used for non-error management-mode messages).
- Quoting in messages uses Unicode curly quotes: `“` (U+201C, `342 200 234`) and `”`
  (U+201D, `342 200 235`). Box-drawing `═` (U+2550) is used in command-help separators.
- No trailing blank line; each message ends with a single `\n`.

Help blocks for colon-commands look like (example `:goto`):

```
 = help: :goto line#|N%|timestamp|#anchor
         ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
           Go to the given location in the top view
```

The `═` rule is 9 spaces + 70 `═` chars. Description is indented 11 spaces.

## 2. File-loading errors (headless `-n`)

### Nonexistent file — exit 1, stderr only, nothing on stdout:

```
  error: unable to open file: /nonexistent/file.log
 reason: No such file or directory
```

(` reason:` line has exactly one leading space; verified byte-for-byte.)

### Permission denied (run as `nobody` against a chmod-000 file) — exit 1:

```
  error: file exists, but is not readable: /tmp/probe/unreadable.log
 reason: Permission denied
```

### Mixed good + bad file args

`lnav -n readable.log /nonexistent.log` (either order): stdout is **empty** (the good
file is *not* dumped), the above two-line error on stderr, exit 1. One bad file aborts
everything.

### Directory argument without `-r`

Loads successfully (no error): every plain file directly inside the dir is loaded and
dumped to stdout in headless mode. Subdirectories are silently ignored. Exit 0.

### Directory with `-r`

Recurses, but **only files matching a known log format are loaded**; unrecognized files
in subdirectories are silently skipped. (Observed: `sub/b.log` containing plain text was
not loaded by `-r`, but `sub/c.log` containing a syslog line was. Given directly, both
load.) No warning is printed for skipped files.

### Unknown log format (headless)

No warning at all: plain unmatched files are treated as text and dumped to stdout;
exit 0. `-W` does not change this. A binary file (NUL bytes) is dumped as a
`hexdump -C`-style view (`  File Offset  00 01 ... ASCII` header row) — exit 0, no
diagnostic.

### Empty file — `-n`: exit 0, no output, no diagnostic.

## 3. `-C` check mode (hidden flag; not shown in `--help`)

Checks each file argument for a detectable log format.

- File matches a format (e.g. syslog line): **no output at all**, exit 0.
- File matches nothing (also: empty file, binary file, a `.json` format file given as
  arg): stderr, exit 1:

  ```
  error:/tmp/probe/readable.log:no format found for file
  ```

  (No leading spaces; absolute path; one line per failing file.)
- Nonexistent file in `-C` mode: the indented `unable to open file` message (as in §2),
  exit 1. When mixed with format failures, the open-error is printed **before** the
  `no format found` lines regardless of argument order.
- Directory argument in `-C` mode: silently ignored, exit 0 (if nothing else fails).
- stdin piped with `-C` (no file args): exit 0, no output (stdin not checked).
- `-C -W` on a matching file: still no output, exit 0.

## 4. Command-line argument errors

All of these print to stderr, prefixed `  error: invalid command-line arguments` with a
` reason:` line. Exit codes vary (CLI11-style codes):

| Case | Exit | ` reason:` |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown flag `-Z` / `--badflag` | 109 | `The following argument was not expected: -Z` |
| `-m help`, `-m exit`, `-m bogus` (unexpected positional) | 109 | `The following argument was not expected: help` |
| `-m config get /global` (extra arg) | 109 | `The following argument was not expected: /global` |
| `-I /nonexistent/dir` | 105 | `-I: Directory does not exist: /nonexistent/dir` |
| `-I readable.log` (a file) | 105 | `-I: Directory is actually a file: readable.log` |
| `-c ''` (empty) | 105 | `-c: empty commands are not allowed` |
| `-c` with no value | 114 | `-c: 1 required  missing` (note double space — empty type name) |
| `-I` with no value | 114 | `-I: 1 required TEXT:DIR missing` |

### `-c` value without type prefix — exit 105, stderr:

```
  error: invalid value for “-c” option
 --> command-line argument
 |  -c foo                                 
 |     ^ command type prefix is missing    
 = help: command arguments must start with one of the following symbols to denote the type of command:
            : - an lnav command   (e.g. :goto 42)
            ; - an SQL statement  (e.g. ;SELECT * FROM syslog_log)
            | - an lnav script    (e.g. |rename-stdin foo)
```

(The two ` | ` lines are space-padded to width 43 like other source lines; caret column
aligns under the value.)

### Bad `-d` debug path

`-d /nonexistent/dir/dbg.log`, `-d /proc/cannotwrite`, `-d <a directory>`: **completely
silent**, exit 0, file loads normally. A valid `-d dbg.log` creates/appends a debug log
(timestamps + `E`/`I` level + source tags), mode `0640`.

### Bad `--since` / `--until` — exit 1, stderr:

```
  error: invalid 'since' time “garbage time”
 reason: Unrecognized input
```

(`-U bogus` gives `invalid 'until' time “bogus”`.)

## 5. `-c` / `-f` command execution errors

**Exit code stays 0** for all command/SQL/script runtime errors below (as long as the
files themselves loaded). Errors go to stderr; multiple `-c` errors are printed in
order with `command-option:N` numbering the Nth `-c`.

### Unknown colon command — stderr, exit 0:

```
  error: unknown command: “nosuchcommand”
```

(curly quotes; nothing else — no source context.)

### SQL syntax/compile errors — stderr, exit 0:

```
  error: failed to compile SQL statement
 reason: incomplete input
 --> command-option:1
 | SELECT bogus FROM                       
```

Other ` reason:` strings observed: `no such column: nosuchcol`,
`no such table: no_such_table`, `no such function: nosuchfunc`.
`';'` alone and `;CREATE TABLE foo (x)` are accepted silently (exit 0).
Successful queries print an ASCII-padded table to **stdout**, e.g. `;SELECT 1 AS x`:

```
    x      
         1 
```

### Bad colon-command arguments — stderr, exit 0; includes help block:

`:filter-in` (no pattern):

```
  error: expecting a regular expression to filter
 --> command-option:1
 | :filter-in                              
 = help: :filter-in pattern
         ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
           Only show lines that match the given regular expression in the
           current view
```

`:filter-in (` (invalid regex) — note source label is `pattern`, plus caret line:

```
  error: “(” is not a valid regular expression
 reason: missing closing parenthesis
 --> pattern
 | (                                       
 |  ^ missing closing parenthesis          
 = help: :filter-in pattern
         ═...
           Only show lines that match the given regular expression in the
           current view
```

`:goto abc`:

```
  error: invalid argument: abc
 reason: expecting line number/percentage, timestamp, or relative time
 --> command-option:1
 | :goto abc                               
 = help: :goto line#|N%|timestamp|#anchor
         ═...
           Go to the given location in the top view
```

`:goto` with no arg, `:goto 999` (past EOF), `:goto -5`: **no error**, exit 0.

### Unknown script via `-c '|name'` or bad `-f` — stderr, exit 0:

```
  error: unknown script -- nosuchscript -- file not found
 --> command-option:1
 | |nosuchscript                           
```

For `-f /nonexistent/cmds.lnav` the ` | ` line shows `|/nonexistent/cmds.lnav`
(`-f file` is internally the command `|file`).

### `-f` script semantics

- `-f <directory>`: silently ignored, exit 0.
- Script lines execute in order; **execution aborts at the first failing line**
  (verified: `:echo FIRST` / `:goto abc` / `:echo THIRD` prints only `FIRST`).
- The error shows **two** source contexts — the command option and the script location
  (absolute path, 1-based line):

```
  error: invalid argument: abc
 reason: expecting line number/percentage, timestamp, or relative time
 --> command-option:1
 | |cmds3.lnav                             
 --> /tmp/probe/cmds3.lnav:2
 | :goto abc                               
 = help: :goto line#|N%|timestamp|#anchor
         ═...
```

### `:echo` prints its argument to **stdout** (`:echo hello world` → `hello world\n`), exit 0.

### `-e` shell commands

The command runs under `/bin/bash -c`-ish; its stdout/stderr become log content.
`lnav -n -e '/nonexistent/cmd-xyz'` → stdout contains
`/bin/bash: line 1: /nonexistent/cmd-xyz: No such file or directory`, exit **0**.
The child’s own exit status (e.g. `exit 3`) does not affect lnav’s exit code.

### `-q` does not suppress any of the above errors (verified with `:goto abc` and nonexistent file).

## 8. `-m` management mode

**`-m` does not read stdin at all** — piping commands (`echo 'help' | lnav -m`) changes
nothing; operations are parsed as CLI arguments. Bare `-m` (or any stdin) → stderr,
exit 1:

```
  error: expecting an operation to perform
 = help: the available operations are:
          • apps: manage lnav apps
          • config: perform operations on the lnav configuration
          • format: perform operations on log file formats
          • piper: perform operations on piper storage
          • regex101: create and edit log message regular expressions using regex101.com
          • crash: manage crash logs
```

(bullet is `•` U+2022, 10-space indent.) `help`, `exit`, `quit` are **not** accepted —
they hit the CLI parser: exit 109 `The following argument was not expected: help`.

Sub-operation listings (all stderr, exit 1, same `  error: ... / = help:` shape):

- `-m config` → `expecting an operation related to lnav configuration`;
  ops: `get`, `blame`, `file-options`.
- `-m format` → `expecting a format name to operate on` + ` = note: the available
  formats are: access_log, alb_log, ...` (72 names, comma-separated, wrapped at ~76
  cols, continuation indent 15 spaces).
- `-m format <name>` → `expecting an operation to perform on the <name> format`
  + ` = note: <name>: <description>` + `            Regexes: rfc5424, std`
  + ops: `get`, `test`, `source`, `sources`, `regex`.
- `-m format <name> regex` → `expecting a regex name to operate on`
  + ` = note: the available regexes are: , rfc5424, std` (note leading empty entry).
- `-m format syslog_log regex std` → `expecting an operation to perform on the std
  regular expression` + ` = help: the available subcommands are:` + `regex101: ...`.
- `-m apps` → `expecting an operation related to lnav apps`; op: `create`.
- `-m piper` → `expecting an operation related to piper storage`; ops: `list`, `clean`.
- `-m crash` → `expecting an operation related to crash logs`; op: `upload`.
- `-m regex101` → `expecting an operation related to the regex101.com integration`;
  ops: `list`, `import`.

Concrete sub-operation behaviors:

- `-m config get` → full JSON config to stdout (9650 lines here, 4-space indent,
  starts `{\n    "$schema": "https://lnav.org/schemas/config-v1.schema.json",`), exit 0.

- `-m format bogusfmt ...` → stderr `  error: unknown format: bogusfmt`, exit 1.
- `-m format syslog_log source[s]` (builtin) → stderr

  format: prints the absolute path on stdout, exit 0.
- `-m format syslog_log regex bogus` → stderr `  error: unknown regex: bogus`, exit 1.
